title: Rotation-days budget enforced at CI; every secret access is audited; audit events carry metadata only
context: Rotation policies that are not enforced quietly slip; audit trails that carry secret bytes turn every log store into a secrets store. Both problems have a fix at the boundary the Secrets Manager client already owns: the client is the sole reader of secret values, so it is the only place that can emit audit events truthfully, and the manifest is the sole declaration of rotation budgets, so CI has one file to enforce against.
decision: Every fetch attempt on the Secrets Manager client emits exactly one structured audit event carrying `{ name, path, environment, principal, outcome, at }`; no field carries the secret value or a substring of it. The audit sink is pluggable behind the same discipline as the wire log; the blueprint fixes the SHAPE of the events, not the storage engine. CI runs the rotation gate (TAC-904) on every change; an entry whose `lastRotatedAt` is more than `rotationDays` in the past fails the run with `SECRETS_ROTATION_EXPIRED`; an entry with no vendor-reported `lastRotatedAt` fails with `SECRETS_ROTATION_UNKNOWN`. An operator-authored override file with an `expiresAt` timestamp is honoured for the named entry until the expiry passes; the override is itself audited every time it applies.
consequences: Rotation cannot silently slip; a CI run is the place the project already gates every change through. Investigating an incident starts with the audit stream and stays there; the log store is safe to ship to a third party because it holds no credential material. The vendor becomes the truth source for rotation age; a vendor without native rotation metadata forces the project into a parallel side-file (an acknowledged trade in TAC-904). The override with an expiry keeps a legitimate mid-rotation change unblocked without opening a permanent bypass; the audited-every-time property makes an over-used override visible.

alternativesConsidered.name: Hash the secret value into audit events for correlation
alternativesConsidered.summary: Emit a stable hash of the value so incident investigators can correlate 'this key was read here and here' without exposing the plaintext.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: A hashed value still lets an attacker with log access confirm 'this hash is the hash for this secret', which is enough for correlation attacks on high-value keys. The event's `name` and `principal` already provide correlation; a hash adds risk without adding capability.

alternativesConsidered.name: Rely on rotation announcements from the vendor rather than a CI gate
alternativesConsidered.summary: Subscribe to the vendor's rotation notification stream and act on drift asynchronously.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Async enforcement is a hope; a synchronous CI gate on every change is the place the project already fails on other drift classes (a lint error, a test failure, a schema mismatch). Enforcing at the same layer keeps the operator experience uniform.

alternativesConsidered.name: Rotate on every deploy
alternativesConsidered.summary: Every merge triggers a full rotation of every secret.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Amplifies blast radius on every deploy failure and makes the vendor's rotation quotas the pacing item. A rotation budget with a bounded override is the honest posture: rotate on the cadence the value's threat model actually needs.
